Taung Horror Hospital

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
After four years under administration, has the North West Department of health improved operation of health facilities like the Taung Community hospital.

Unique Selling Point:
The Taung Community Hospital is the go-to place for many villagers in the north west who need medical attention. It is also, according to some of its previous and current patients, a place where the desperate go to die. We investigate why the facility has led down patients despite overnemnt's several attempts to improve it under administration.

Summary:
The North West health department is still failing the people of the province despite being placed on administration four years ago. The intervention dates back to 2018 when governemnt invoked section 100 of the constitution following corruption and a lack of service delivery. On the ground this is what it looked like:


Residents were complaining of medicine shortages
Shortages of ambulance services, and even if there are, the very few that were operating werent able to reach far flung villages due to bad roads.
The filling in of posts or lack thereof
And people complained about the Gupta linked Mediosa scheme which led to the purchase of mobile clinics. The trucks, all valued at R30 million, have specialised equipment such as X-ray machines and tools for dental services but have rarely been used. They are gathering dust following investigations about tender processes etc.


All these problems and more led to widespread protests hence the need to place the department on administration. Now, the big story currently is that the period under administration is set to come to an end and everyone is asking the question - have things improved. That essentially will be our angle for the story - using the Taung hospital as our case in point via the stories of people who say they received terrible service there.


Further information:
Dr Jeanette Hunter, Deputy Director of Primary Healthcare in the National Department of Health, was appointed as administrator for the North West health department. And she says that it’s all systems go. She believes there have been some significant changes or improvements that warrant the lifting of the section 100 intervention. But health workers and residents disagree.

Irrespective, Hunter who has been overseeing the project highlighted five areas that have improved:

Vacancies have been filled - as mentioned earlier this was a big problem four years ago. According to the exit report by Hunter, this was looked at. She says The vacancy rate has been brought down from 19% to 11%. In fact, Five thousand posts have been filled since the national government’s intervention. This is according to MEC Madoda Smabatha, who presented his 2022/23 budget speech last month. He said 1,121 permanent posts were filled in the previous (2021/22) financial year, and that the progress made in filling posts will go a long way in improving the capacity of the department to effectively deliver on its mandate.
But health workers and residents say this has not led to much needed relief as facility managers, including the one at Taung hospital say they still struggle with staff shortages,

One area that was flagged as a concern after the inter-ministerial task team’s oversight visit last year, was emergency medical services. In 2018, there were only 50 functional ambulances. This had increased to 147 by 2021. According to national standards, 350 EMS vehicles are required to service the province. BUT it will take up to seven years for the North West to reach this level. At present, the province is operating with 138 ambulances. And even with that kind of a fleet ambulances are not able to reach people.

Record keeping is another concern. Poor record-keeping remains a problem in the department because they are still using a manual system which leads to a delay in payments, keeping track of financial transactions and staff records.

Next issue - Availability of medicine has also been a persistent challenge in the province. On paper this has been sorted but we still have residents, who we will interview who say they visit the hospital and come out with no medicine. There are medicine stockouts. Mothers reporting that their kids skip their infancy vaccines because they are not available. There are still shortages in ARV or TB treatments. People are sent home without them.

Financially, the department had not grown its accruals over the past four years. Accruals are funds that were supposed to be paid to suppliers in a specific financial year, but were carried over to the next financial year due to a lack of funding. Currently, annual accruals still hover around the R1.2-billion mark. Though the North West treasury has allocated R350-million to help finance the accruals, the challenges of insufficient budget allocations remain. The department has also underspent its budget by 1%. Roughly R14-billion health budget for the province in the 2020/21 financial year, the department underspent by R144-million. The underspending was mainly on the health facilities’ revitalisation grant, which means money that the department had for new facilities, upgrades, refurbishments or maintenance was not spent in full.

Press Release:


Ailing and Abetting - Taung District Hospital
Managers who forget to pay suppliers on time. Medicine stockouts. A million-rand container clinic in dire condition and a hospital providing patchy service to patients living in an area with no other healthcare options. In our series on the true state of state health, Carte Blanche sets off for Taung District Hospital in North West. After four years under the administration by the National Department of Health, are the people of Taung finally getting the state healthcare they need?
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


VO - “No woman should die while giving a life. And no child should die of preventable diseases”.


A bold commitment to patients arriving at a hospital serving poverty-stricken villages in Taung, in the North West…


And a commitment many patients say doctors and nursing staff here are failing to live up to.

In the maternity wards, women wait unattended in long queues – sometimes left to deliver babies on their own… as this video filmed in January so horrifyingly shows.


LET THE VIDEO BREATH - BOOST THE LADY IN THE VIDEO CALLING FOR HELP.


The chaos isn’t confined to the maternity ward. Filming under cover, we reveal a hospital in dire need of an upgrade – not to mention more linen and food.

They’re among the many reasons some residents no longer come here for help. 42 year old Tsholofelo Meko, a mother of two, is one of them.

SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO


23:17 I no longer go to the clinic to tell you the truth I never go back there. The youngest burnt herself
with tea the other day. I told myself that I’ll treat her myself and if she dies she will rather die in my care 23:35.
VO - Meko’s grievance with Taung Hospital has a 14-year history: She blames the facility for having to bury both her mom and her epileptic three-year-old son in 2009.

SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO

07:00 He was admitted into the hospital because he had fits. They ran multiple tests and
they told me that they can’t figure out what is causing the fits.
07:14 Okay, I was there when they were doing the tests, drawing his blood every day
and taking it to the laboratory. When the results came back they still couldn’t tell what’s going
on.

VO – It’s been more than a decade, but Meko says the pain of those experiences is kept alive by the additional trauma she endured.

SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO

11:10 Sometimes when I was at the hospital, his fits would start, but the nurses wouldn’t be there. I would have to leave my child unattended and run to call them from their offices where they would be just sitting and busy chatting away.
19:24 There aren’t enough doctors at that hospital. You can’t have one doctor work all of the wards. When you’re in a ward you have to wait for a doctor that’s busy working at another ward.

VO - She recalls how doctors at Taung dismissed her concerns, instead referring her to Klerksdorp hospital 234 kilometers away - a costly exercise for someone surviving on a government grant.

SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO

08:19 The doctor there said the doctors at Taung don’t know how to do their job. He said they should have written a full medical history. Because they don’t understand what tests they did and what they mean.
VO - She was sent back to the Taung hospital…
SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO

08:43 On the bottom of the medical file, the Klerksdoorp doctor wrote “Do your work doctor”.

VO - Meko eventually decided to take him home. But his health deteriorated.
SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO

12:36. He started fitting. I was sitting on the couch and I laid a blanket for him on the floor. I was alone at the time. 12:53 I just watched him. I then asked my sister to check him and she said he’s gone.

Masa Link - clip P100694.MOV

Listening to Tsholofelo describe how she lay a blanket on the floor alone in her house and
watched her baby die , it’s heartbreaking. And that is an understatement. But something I
also noticed there's almost a theme of being desensitised to death. And it’s not because
she’s not hurt, definitely not. It’s because of a system that has failed her schedule many
times. That she has become desensitised.

VO - It was stories like Tsholofelo’s that compelled us to investigate what was happening in the region.

What we found was a health system in crisis – with residents complaining of a critical shortage of ambulances and medicines and having to walk long distances to clinics.
Masa Link - Clip P1007001

Behind me is the Cokonyane clinic. It’s a container. And it’s supposed to service the residents Of this area and surrounding villages that is a lot of people people here complain about lack of medicine lack of quality services lack of staff it’s dirty and it’s just not the kind of place that they say you would want to send your loved one to when they are such. This container?!
VO – It’s a container that costs the North West Health Department nearly R1,2 million. Although our spy cam footage shows it’s in a dire condition.

The sick are expected to use these dirty toilets and to queue outside before being attended to by one health official.


VO - The province’s MEC for Health, Madoda Sambatha, blames the condition of the Taung hospital and the Cokonyane clinic on incompetent staff.


MEC INTERVIEW SOUND UP

Masa 21:05 As you are speaking of improvements this is the condition of the toilets
(Masa showing MEC dirty toilets on her phone) …this is the loo the woman in this area , when they go to the clinic, use. What do you have to say about that?

MEC 21:53 I do what it’s called unannounced visits and I will go to that Clinic that you telling me about in Ratlou . On my arrival heads are going to roll. Some of the issues it’s not because we don’t have the money. it is because managers at times themselves are not properly delivering on what they are expected to do.


VO – Those same managers, the MEC says, also forgot to pay suppliers on time, leading to severe medicine shortages in various facilities.

SOUND UP MEC INTERVIEW

MEC 29:07 it’s historical and an issue of management. Historical, in the fact that there was a time when we discovered that we were owing almost 75 companies who had been contracted to supply medicine. What they did was to put our department on hold. What we discovered is that most of the invoices were in the drawers of people in the medical store.

MASA 30:00 So you have the medicine, it’s just not getting to the facility?

MEC: That’s what I’m saying to you.

VO - But this is about more than medicine shortages. Medupe Tshilo is another aggrieved resident who says it’s not unusual for nurses to delegate tasks to patients’ families.

SOUND UP- MEDUPE TSHILO

12:31 Just this week on Tuesday, I took my brother to the hospital. They made a referral letter for us at the clinic to Taung Hospital.
13:26 When we got to the ward they asked us to take off his clothes and dress him in hospital clothes. We had to do that ourselves and I asked them why they’ve giving us their work to do. 14:30 and they said that we should put a diaper on him and asked why they didn't give him a crutch so he could use the bathroom on his own when he needed to, but they refused and they said we should put it on.
VO – Plagued by these and other problems, the North West Health Department was placed under administration in 2018 to be overseen by the National Department, and help ensure the province meets the national standards for providing healthcare services.

The department was told to fill vacancies, improve its record-keeping system, address the medicine shortages and, most importantly, boost its ambulance fleet.
VO - Medupe also recalls how - after waiting for 12 hours - his 80-year-old aunt, Lydia Jotdwe, died in an ambulance on her way to Taung hospital.
SOUND UP - MEDUPE TSHILO

07:17 It was chaotic because we just couldn’t understand why the ambulance took so long to fetch a person and had they come in time maybe she would’ve been saved at the hospital.


Masa Link - Clip P1006991.MOV

01:48:00:18 Medupi is like many residents here who rely on the public transport system and live off social grants. So they don’t have money. They don’t have the luxury of hopping into the car and going into the clinic or hospital. So they have to wait for that ambulance. Even if it takes 12 hours.

VO – Desperately needing to get to Taung Hospital, Rinah Mohitleng, was left stranded after going into labour at night - an inconvenient time for any pregnant woman living in this village.


SOUND UP- RINAH MOHITHLENG
03:24 I called the ambulance at night when I started feeling the pains but there
were no ambulances available.
VO - With no way to pay for the R400 private trip, Mohihleng was forced to wait until sunrise. When she arrived, her baby was still born.



SOUND UP- RINAH MOHITHLENG

02:59 They take a long time to check on pregnant women. So by the time they got to me, they took me to the ultrasound and they said the child’s heart is no longer beating.

VO - Meko also believes her mother could have been saved had she not been left unattended by the hospital staff.
SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO

17:09 I realised that they hadn’t given my mother a bath. She had been there for a week but she had developed bedsores on her back because they weren’t turning her enough 17:25
18:26 I went back there one day and found my mother in a bad state. She was now eating with the pipe and I thought she actually thought to myself that she looked worse.

VO – Due to exit administration next month, questions are being asked about whether the department has been rehabilitated, given unresolved problems like the ambulance shortage.

MASA QUESTION 07:14 The picture that you are painting and the reality of these people on the ground are night and day. Pregnant women are still giving birth on the corridor, ambulances are far and wide. In fact, we didn’t even see a single one in our time here and we were even inside of the hospital. Residents are complaining about basic services that should be given, like a lack of medication, All the reasons you got into administration in the first place are seemingly still there till today.

MEC 09:21 If you go to EMS 100 ambulances have been purchased.
Masa 09:27 where are they? Where are these ambulances that you speak of. I’m saying I was there and I didn’t see a single ambulance.
09:58 In terms of the national norm if we were to be doing well on Ambulance availability we would have 403 ambulances on each day available.rFt
10:18 We only have 188 available. In the budget speech I indicated that the manner in which we are procuring ambulances will take 7 years to have that 400 If we do it. But we decided to change it so that in the next intake we purchase ambulances.

MASA 11:31 You acknowledge MEC that there is a severe shortage of
ambulances…11:43 you acknowledge that?
11:48 I am confirming yes indeed, according to norms and standards. In fact if you take it on budget allocation, our allocation only allows us to purchase 50 ambulances per
annum.

VO - In fact, 350 ambulances that are required to service the province, according to the national norms and standards.

188 is nothing close to the 350 EMS vehicles required, according to the national standards. Irrespective, the MEC believes the province is ready to operate independently again.
00:45 The administration is gradually getting out as per the decision of cabinet, as a department we are ready to be out of that. 06:33 There is an element of success and if you want to ask me, I would say the
administration, the onus is on us and the department to ensure that which has been done, keeps on improving.


VO – But to a community describing itself as forgotten by his department, the MEC’s promises are cold comfort.

Masa Link - Clip P1007001 Behind me is the Cokonyane clinic. It’s a container. And it’s supposed to service the residents Of this area and surrounding villages that is a lot of people people here complain about lack of medicine lack of quality services lack of staff it’s dirty and it’s just not the kind of place that they say you would want to send your loved one to when they are such. This container?! VO – It’s a container that costs the North West Health Department nearly R1,2 million. Although our spy cam footage shows it’s in a dire condition. The sick are expected to use these dirty toilets and to queue outside before being attended to by one health official. VO - The province’s MEC for Health, Madoda Sambatha, blames the condition of the Taung hospital and the Cokonyane clinic on incompetent staff. MEC INTERVIEW SOUND UP Masa 21:05 As you are speaking of improvements this is the condition of the toilets (Masa showing MEC dirty toilets on her phone) …this is the loo the woman in this area , when they go to the clinic, use. What do you have to say about that? MEC 21:53 I do what it’s called unannounced visits and I will go to that Clinic that you telling me about in Ratlou . On my arrival heads are going to roll. Some of the issues it’s not because we don’t have the money. it is because managers at times themselves are not properly delivering on what they are expected to do. VO – Those same managers, the MEC says, also forgot to pay suppliers on time, leading to severe medicine shortages in various facilities. SOUND UP MEC INTERVIEW MEC 29:07 it’s historical and an issue of management. Historical, in the fact that there was a time when we discovered that we were owing almost 75 companies who had been contracted to supply medicine. What they did was to put our department on hold. What we discovered is that most of the invoices were in the drawers of people in the medical store. MASA 30:00 So you have the medicine, it’s just not getting to the facility? MEC: That’s what I’m saying to you. VO - But this is about more than medicine shortages. Medupe Tshilo is another aggrieved resident who says it’s not unusual for nurses to delegate tasks to patients’ families. SOUND UP- MEDUPE TSHILO 12:31 Just this week on Tuesday, I took my brother to the hospital. They made a referral letter for us at the clinic to Taung Hospital. 13:26 When we got to the ward they asked us to take off his clothes and dress him in hospital clothes. We had to do that ourselves and I asked them why they’ve giving us their work to do. 14:30 and they said that we should put a diaper on him and asked why they didn't give him a crutch so he could use the bathroom on his own when he needed to, but they refused and they said we should put it on. VO – Plagued by these and other problems, the North West Health Department was placed under administration in 2018 to be overseen by the National Department, and help ensure the province meets the national standards for providing healthcare services. The department was told to fill vacancies, improve its record-keeping system, address the medicine shortages and, most importantly, boost its ambulance fleet. VO - Medupe also recalls how - after waiting for 12 hours - his 80-year-old aunt, Lydia Jotdwe, died in an ambulance on her way to Taung hospital. SOUND UP - MEDUPE TSHILO 07:17 It was chaotic because we just couldn’t understand why the ambulance took so long to fetch a person and had they come in time maybe she would’ve been saved at the hospital. Masa Link - Clip P1006991.MOV 01:48:00:18 Medupi is like many residents here who rely on the public transport system and live off social grants. So they don’t have money. They don’t have the luxury of hopping into the car and going into the clinic or hospital. So they have to wait for that ambulance. Even if it takes 12 hours. VO – Desperately needing to get to Taung Hospital, Rinah Mohitleng, was left stranded after going into labour at night - an inconvenient time for any pregnant woman living in this village. SOUND UP- RINAH MOHITHLENG 03:24 I called the ambulance at night when I started feeling the pains but there were no ambulances available. VO - With no way to pay for the R400 private trip, Mohihleng was forced to wait until sunrise. When she arrived, her baby was still born. SOUND UP- RINAH MOHITHLENG 02:59 They take a long time to check on pregnant women. So by the time they got to me, they took me to the ultrasound and they said the child’s heart is no longer beating. VO - Meko also believes her mother could have been saved had she not been left unattended by the hospital staff. SOUND UP- TSHOLOFELO MEKO 17:09 I realised that they hadn’t given my mother a bath. She had been there for a week but she had developed bedsores on her back because they weren’t turning her enough 17:25 18:26 I went back there one day and found my mother in a bad state. She was now eating with the pipe and I thought she actually thought to myself that she looked worse. VO – Due to exit administration next month, questions are being asked about whether the department has been rehabilitated, given unresolved problems like the ambulance shortage. MASA QUESTION 07:14 The picture that you are painting and the reality of these people on the ground are night and day. Pregnant women are still giving birth on the corridor, ambulances are far and wide. In fact, we didn’t even see a single one in our time here and we were even inside of the hospital. Residents are complaining about basic services that should be given, like a lack of medication, All the reasons you got into administration in the first place are seemingly still there till today. MEC 09:21 If you go to EMS 100 ambulances have been purchased. Masa 09:27 where are they? Where are these ambulances that you speak of. I’m saying I was there and I didn’t see a single ambulance. 09:58 In terms of the national norm if we were to be doing well on Ambulance availability we would have 403 ambulances on each day available.rFt 10:18 We only have 188 available. In the budget speech I indicated that the manner in which we are procuring ambulances will take 7 years to have that 400 If we do it. But we decided to change it so that in the next intake we purchase ambulances. MASA 11:31 You acknowledge MEC that there is a severe shortage of ambulances…11:43 you acknowledge that? 11:48 I am confirming yes indeed, according to norms and standards. In fact if you take it on budget allocation, our allocation only allows us to purchase 50 ambulances per annum. VO - In fact, 350 ambulances that are required to service the province, according to the national norms and standards. 188 is nothing close to the 350 EMS vehicles required, according to the national standards. Irrespective, the MEC believes the province is ready to operate independently again. 00:45 The administration is gradually getting out as per the decision of cabinet, as a department we are ready to be out of that. 06:33 There is an element of success and if you want to ask me, I would say the administration, the onus is on us and the department to ensure that which has been done, keeps on improving. VO – But to a community describing itself as forgotten by his department, the MEC’s promises are cold comfort.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): After four years under administration, has the North West Department of health improved operation of health facilities like the Taung Community hospital.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Taung Community Hospital is the go-to place for many villagers in the north west who need medical attention. It is also, according to some of its previous and current patients, a place where the desperate go to die. We investigate why the facility has led down patients despite overnemnt's several attempts to improve it under administration.
metadata.Summary: The North West health department is still failing the people of the province despite being placed on administration four years ago. The intervention dates back to 2018 when governemnt invoked section 100 of the constitution following corruption and a lack of service delivery. On the ground this is what it looked like: Residents were complaining of medicine shortages Shortages of ambulance services, and even if there are, the very few that were operating werent able to reach far flung villages due to bad roads. The filling in of posts or lack thereof And people complained about the Gupta linked Mediosa scheme which led to the purchase of mobile clinics. The trucks, all valued at R30 million, have specialised equipment such as X-ray machines and tools for dental services but have rarely been used. They are gathering dust following investigations about tender processes etc. All these problems and more led to widespread protests hence the need to place the department on administration. Now, the big story currently is that the period under administration is set to come to an end and everyone is asking the question - have things improved. That essentially will be our angle for the story - using the Taung hospital as our case in point via the stories of people who say they received terrible service there.
metadata.Further information: Dr Jeanette Hunter, Deputy Director of Primary Healthcare in the National Department of Health, was appointed as administrator for the North West health department. And she says that it’s all systems go. She believes there have been some significant changes or improvements that warrant the lifting of the section 100 intervention. But health workers and residents disagree. Irrespective, Hunter who has been overseeing the project highlighted five areas that have improved: Vacancies have been filled - as mentioned earlier this was a big problem four years ago. According to the exit report by Hunter, this was looked at. She says The vacancy rate has been brought down from 19% to 11%. In fact, Five thousand posts have been filled since the national government’s intervention. This is according to MEC Madoda Smabatha, who presented his 2022/23 budget speech last month. He said 1,121 permanent posts were filled in the previous (2021/22) financial year, and that the progress made in filling posts will go a long way in improving the capacity of the department to effectively deliver on its mandate. But health workers and residents say this has not led to much needed relief as facility managers, including the one at Taung hospital say they still struggle with staff shortages, One area that was flagged as a concern after the inter-ministerial task team’s oversight visit last year, was emergency medical services. In 2018, there were only 50 functional ambulances. This had increased to 147 by 2021. According to national standards, 350 EMS vehicles are required to service the province. BUT it will take up to seven years for the North West to reach this level. At present, the province is operating with 138 ambulances. And even with that kind of a fleet ambulances are not able to reach people. Record keeping is another concern. Poor record-keeping remains a problem in the department because they are still using a manual system which leads to a delay in payments, keeping track of financial transactions and staff records. Next issue - Availability of medicine has also been a persistent challenge in the province. On paper this has been sorted but we still have residents, who we will interview who say they visit the hospital and come out with no medicine. There are medicine stockouts. Mothers reporting that their kids skip their infancy vaccines because they are not available. There are still shortages in ARV or TB treatments. People are sent home without them. Financially, the department had not grown its accruals over the past four years. Accruals are funds that were supposed to be paid to suppliers in a specific financial year, but were carried over to the next financial year due to a lack of funding. Currently, annual accruals still hover around the R1.2-billion mark. Though the North West treasury has allocated R350-million to help finance the accruals, the challenges of insufficient budget allocations remain. The department has also underspent its budget by 1%. Roughly R14-billion health budget for the province in the 2020/21 financial year, the department underspent by R144-million. The underspending was mainly on the health facilities’ revitalisation grant, which means money that the department had for new facilities, upgrades, refurbishments or maintenance was not spent in full.
